en: Appeared before his eyes.
When he saw brave Seytek,
His blood surged and raced,
And his beloved protector came into view.
Strength entered him; grinding his teeth,
The doomed man said:
“My protector has come—so be it!
If I now die at the hands
Of a warrior mighty in terror, my heart is content.
My valiant one has appeared before my eyes;
If I die now, I have no regret,
Not the smallest regret remains in me.
If I should die suddenly,
If by chance my time has come,
There is one who will seize and fold me at the waist,
One I trust as my support,
Who will load me for the journey to Ala-Too.
He will not let the beasts devour me,
Nor let it be said that Joltoy died
At the hands of the merciless.
He will not harbor dreadful thoughts,
Nor let wolves tear flesh from my haunches,
Nor allow the fanged beasts
To dishonor my soul in the end.
‘Dig and turn the earth with a mattock—
Seytek has come, bury me,’” he said.
Placing his hope in the young man,
He was wholly freed from anxiety;
No longer fearing the Chinese calamity,
His spirits lifted and his heart grew calm.
“My protector has visibly come;
As I depart this world,
I have seen my beloved one,” he thought.
Taking heart, he braced himself.
Seeing the gray wolf, Akjoltoy
Counted that lone hero as a host;
His anguish subsided,
And hope in his fleeting life returned.
His sorrowful heart relaxed,
And Joltoy stood watching.
He saw a broad-chested figure,
Seeming like a bridge across a mighty river,
Guarding all the people.
That falcon born a champion,
Whose fathers and forefathers
Had never retreated before an enemy,
Tightened and buckled his war belt,
Then attacked the ninety-four.
A roar of shouting rose before him;
The valor of the young champion blazed
As he invoked his ancestors in his battle cry:
“In this holy war,
Support me, my own heroic father!
My forefather Manas the lion,
Make straight the path before me now!”
Upon his mountain-like gray horse,
In his billowing golden coat,
He poured out his wrath, grim-faced.
The gray war belt inherited from his forefathers
Blazed brightly, fastened around his waist.
Like a prince ruling a nation,
He rejoiced when he saw the champion,
Like a man beholding at her wedding feast
His maiden beloved, the beautiful Bermet.
His mighty teeth, broad as a gate,
Showed within his mouth,
While blue smoke thick as an arm
Streamed from the corners of his lips.
Charging downhill, the hero speared
The ninety-four who met him;
Among the Chinese who pressed upon him,
Each bore the fury of a thousand,
Each was a black demon incarnate,
Yet he skewered them two at a time.
Of the forefathers who had gone before,
Which one could have struck more fiercely?
He made Kulansur prance,
And laid low all who faced him.
Those he grappled with he never released;
Some of those champions
Could never be filled though feasts were cooked,
And once they fought, they spared no life.
Their prowess surpassed all others;
They stood foremost before the khan,
Champions of deadly venom.
Swearing to devour the Burut whole,
They had made their pledge firm
And readied every piece of armor.
Of the warriors who came from Beijing,
No fewer than fourteen giants lay dead;
The Chinese advance was cut off.
As the battle raged on,
Chongbilgich roared aloud,
Thundering and surging into fury.
He was said to be the son of Kün-Jangjung,
And they called him Küpü the Wrestler.
He was immensely strong in a grapple;
When he seized a man in combat,
He would twist and break his neck.
He could overturn a mountain in his path
And uproot anyone he encountered;
If a man fled, he never escaped.
He confronted all whose death had come.
His prowess was renowned:
“He is the son of Ai-Jangjung,
This is the warrior from Beijing
Destined for the khan’s golden throne,”
So it was entered in his record.
“He is the greatest of forty tribes;
The misery of every enemy
Who meets him will boil without end.”
His valor was well known;
Clairvoyants in Beijing
And judges of men had tested him.
His nose was like a mountain spur;
He drew breath like a dragon,
As though he could devour the entire world.
His eyes were blue as steel;
When you looked upon his nose,
It resembled a ridge where a rich lord camped.
The black brows above his eyes
Were like a mastiff barking at the fold.
None dared advance against him;
His nature was vicious, his presence terrible,
And no man dared provoke him.
On foot he was a wrestler of surpassing might,
With iron hands trained to perfection.
When he looked upon a human face,
Anyone who confronted him
Seemed to die before death itself.
He was the hero who tore apart nine giants.
There was also a man called Jangyzköz,
Who, they said, paid neither tribute nor tax
And yielded to no word spoken.
He ravaged and destroyed foreign peoples,
A hero who swallowed every giant he fought.
Roaming ceaselessly and ranging over the land,
He was a warrior who smelled of dust.
He was a man reeking of blood,
His valor was beyond compare,
A hellish figure when enraged,
His prowess was immense,
A hero worthy of girding at the waist,
Not merely the white-capped Kyrgyz people,
But the whole wide world he would subdue,
And bring to ruin, they said.
He was that lord, that hero,
When he waged war against the khagan,
That lion wielded a steel mace.
Against the infidel son of Ai-Zhangzhung,
Seytek, that mountain-like hero,
Before one could cry out,
Before a sentence could be finished,
Before one could pinch one’s nose,
Before a closed eye could open,
The socketed spear Syrnaiza,
Which would not recoil even from striking stone,
Whenever it found its mark,
Never returned without shattering it.
Upon the heroic son of Ai-Zhangzhung
He came from the flank,
Thinking, “Here is the point of the elbow,
Here in a living man are the lungs,
And here is the very windpipe.
If the Creator grants me honor,
Now is the moment to overturn him.”
That ever-ready hero
Measured and fixed upon the spot,
With matchless swiftness,
And drove the splendid steel Syrnaiza
Into the chosen place.
When he struck, they collided,
The iron-black charger
And Seytek’s Kulansur
Sank knee-deep into the sand,
The spear broke apart with a crash,
White splinters as large as a nomad’s hut
Flew rattling into the sky,
And the mighty son of Zhangzhung’s
Supporting stirrup strap
Was torn clean through.
His deep-blue iron helmet
Flew off and struck the ground.
There was a battle-axe with a steel head
In Seytek’s hand,
Its haft entwined with gold,
Its lamb-liver-shaped blade was keen steel,
Forged and honed by gathered masters.
So no place it struck would remain unharmed,
But would fester and grow inflamed,
So that the death of one it gashed
Would come within a mare’s milking,
His gall would burst and his soul burn,
And he would depart this world,
They had whetted its edge,
In the venom of a dragon
And the deadly vapor of a ravenous demon
They had tempered it sixty times,
And any mortal whom it touched
It instantly robbed of life;
Such was the Oikuma in his hand.
The most nimble and skillful champion,
A wise man versed in every stratagem,
Your finest gray wolf of war,
Grasped it by the haft,
Drew Oikuma from its sheath,
Skillfully swung the blade,
And struck the heroic son of Ai-Zhangzhung
Upon the head;
His head split in two,
The champion’s blood poured out,
And like a collapsing mountain
He toppled from his horse.
When the champion fell from his mount,
When he came crashing to the ground,
Er Bilgich, son of Kojozhash,
A destroyer surpassing all mortals,
A sorcerous archer,
Cried, “Now I am left alone!
There were ninety men as great as mountains,
Though all ninety might die,
Kaisar alone was a true hero.
Among the coat-clad Chinese
He was the son of the strongest,
From the pure breed that girded itself with stone,
He surpassed even the great.
He met the enemy and was destroyed;
Our dream has turned ill.
Our khan died before even striking—
Has such a thing ever happened in all the ages?
Deprived of our renowned champion,
Our forces are thrown into distress.
Our splendid hero Kaisar is gone,
And now our backbone is broken.
Having let the Kyrgyz triumph
And surrendered mighty Kaisar
To those accursed Burut,
How can we retreat without shame?
What answer shall we give
To our great leader Kite?”
So saying, Chongbilgich
Roared out his grief,
And every mortal who heard him
Shuddered from head to foot.
Pale and ashen,
Wild with fury and scowling,
He loomed, scattering his wrath;
The wretched warrior from the khagan’s realm
Reared like a towering mountain.
The sorcerous warrior-hero
Truly brought on the end of the age;
His valor became plain
When he roared and charged—
Not only men but beasts,
Champions with strength upon strength,
Overwhelming, conquering monsters,
